interactions.label: Why is transvaginal ultrasound preferred over transabdominal ultrasound as first

params.question: Why is transvaginal ultrasound preferred over transabdominal ultrasound as first-line pelvic imaging in a sexually active woman of reproductive age?

answers.text: It uses no ionising radiation, and its endovaginal probe sits close to the ovaries and uterus, giving superior resolution of small structures.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Many reproductive-age women may already be pregnant, so a radiation-free test is preferred, and the close probe position gives the finer resolution needed for follicles and small pelvic structures.

answers.text: It is the only modality that can establish a diagnosis of polycystic ovarian disease without any clinical criteria.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ultrasound is only one of three Rotterdam criteria for polycystic ovarian disease and cannot make the diagnosis alone. Clinical and biochemical features are still required.

answers.text: The transabdominal probe operates at a higher frequency, so it counts antral follicles more accurately.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transabdominal ultrasound has lower resolution, which is why follicle counting becomes unreliable and ovarian volume is used instead. The higher-resolution endovaginal probe is the one that suits follicle counting.

answers.text: It measures serum androgen levels directly, so the free androgen index does not need to be checked separately.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ultrasound measures anatomy and does not measure hormone levels. Hyperandrogenism is assessed clinically and biochemically, so the free androgen index is still needed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three reasons for TVS: no ionising radiation, a probe close to the pelvic organs, and superior resolution. Transabdominal scanning is reserved as the fallback.
Transvaginal ultrasound combines the absence of radiation with high-resolution imaging at close range, which is why it is first-line in the reproductive-age woman.

params.question: A 27-year-old has a positive pregnancy test, lower abdominal pain and a serum beta hCG of 3,000 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with no gestational sac. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

answers.text: An ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, because the beta hCG is above the discriminatory zone.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A normally rising beta hCG crosses the discriminatory zone of about 1,500 to 2,000 IU/L, and a gestational sac should be visible in the uterus by then, so an empty uterus at this level is a tubal ectopic until proven otherwise.

answers.text: An early intrauterine pregnancy that is too small to visualise, so the scan should be repeated in two weeks.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At this hormone level a normal intrauterine pregnancy should already be visible, so waiting two weeks risks a ruptured tubal ectopic. Delayed reassessment is only appropriate when beta hCG is below the discriminatory zone.

answers.text: A pseudosac, which is a normal early finding and can be safely ignored.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A pseudosac is a fluid collection in the endometrial cavity that mimics a gestational sac, so it must never be used to reassure. It has no yolk sac and no double decidual sign, so it does not rule out an ectopic.

answers.text: Normal physiological endometrial thickening, with reassurance and repeat beta hCG at 48 hours.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An empty uterus is not normal endometrial change in a pregnancy with a rising beta hCG. A rising hormone level with an empty uterus must be treated as ectopic, not monitored passively.

overallFeedback.feedback: The discriminatory zone is the key reference point. Above it, an empty uterus means ectopic until proven otherwise, not reassurance or a delayed repeat.
Read every scan against the beta hCG. An empty uterus above the discriminatory zone makes an ectopic highly likely until it is excluded.

params.question: A 22-year-old has oligo-anovulation and a raised free androgen index. Her transvaginal scan shows polycystic ovarian morphology. Which statement about the scan is correct?

answers.text: The scan is confirmatory rather than essential, because two Rotterdam criteria are already met, provided mimics such as thyroid disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing syndrome and hyperprolactinaemia have been excluded.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rotterdam needs any two of three criteria, and this patient already has two clinical features. The scan adds confirmation, but only after mimics are excluded.

answers.text: The scan is mandatory, because ultrasound is one of the criteria that must always be met for the diagnosis.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ultrasound is one of three possible criteria, and any two are sufficient. The scan is not a mandatory element when two clinical criteria are already present.

answers.text: Polycystic morphology alone establishes the diagnosis, so the clinical and biochemical features are not needed.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Polycystic morphology on ultrasound is only one criterion. On its own it is an incidental finding that warrants metabolic monitoring, not a diagnosis.

answers.text: The diagnosis can be made directly from the scan without excluding thyroid disease, adrenal or pituitary causes, because the scan is the final arbiter.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mimics such as thyroid disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing syndrome and hyperprolactinaemia must be excluded before the diagnosis is made. Imaging cannot exclude these endocrine causes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the Rotterdam rule: any two of oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic morphology, after excluding mimics. The scan provides only one of the three.
Rotterdam needs any two of three criteria, after excluding mimics. Here the clinical features already satisfy two criteria, so the scan confirms rather than makes the diagnosis.

interactions.label: A couple's hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal block with no spill into

params.question: A couple's hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal block with no spill into the peritoneal cavity. Semen analysis is normal, and the uterine cavity is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: In-vitro fertilisation, because it bypasses the blocked tubes.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bilateral tubal block means natural conception and intrauterine insemination are not viable, and IVF bypasses the tubes entirely.

answers.text: Intrauterine insemination, because the couple needs only one patent tube.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intrauterine insemination needs at least one patent tube. Here both tubes are blocked, so sperm cannot reach the oocyte through them.

answers.text: Hysteroscopic polypectomy, because a cavity lesion must be removed before any treatment.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hysteroscopic removal is indicated for a polyp or submucous fibroid. The cavity here is normal, so there is no lesion to correct.

answers.text: Timed intercourse with ovulation induction, because tubal block is usually a mild problem.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Timed intercourse needs at least one patent tube so that the sperm and oocyte can meet. Bilateral block makes natural conception impossible, regardless of ovulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Work through the tubes first. Bilateral block bypasses natural conception and insemination, so IVF is the route, not cavity surgery or ovulation induction.
Tubal patency decides the route. Bilateral block points to IVF, while a patent side leaves options such as IUI.
